schools.summary: Gill supplies the condition the plan relied on and is astonished that the elders voted for it.
Henry names the strategy, hears a general ruin called a general peace, and sets the counsel beside that of Caiaphas.
Clarke states the counterfactual of twelve thousand picked men, and Wesley repeats Henry's contrast with two additions of his own.
Ellicott judges the advice sound and raises a difficulty about the timing; Keil and Delitzsch note that Hushai was sent for all the same.

debates.question: Was Ahithophel's plan as good as it looked?

sides.position: So good that only a miraculous interposition could have saved David from it
Sound, and proved so by the trouble taken to defeat it and to warn David
Sound in strategy, and right about David's weakness at that moment

outliers.note: Alone in objecting that David was already at the fords, further off than a single day's march from Jerusalem.

1.pericope_label: Let me now choose out twelve thousand men; the saying pleased Absalom

schools.summary: Gill ascribes the calling of a second counsellor to providence blinding the prince's mind.
Clarke comments on the she-bear of the comparison, and Wesley on a God who can arm a man against himself.
Ellicott states the facts without the theology, and Keil and Delitzsch render the answer and reject a proposed reading of its verb.

debates.question: Why was Hushai called in at all?

sides.position: Providence blinded the prince at the one point where clear sight would have served him
There is no contending with a God who can destroy a man by his own mistakes and passions
Ordinary prudence: a second opinion at an important crisis

outliers.note: Alone in commenting on the she-bear of the comparison, with a promise of instances at the end of the chapter.

themes: a bear robbed of her whelps
5.pericope_label: Call now Hushai the Archite; the counsel of Ahithophel is not good at this time

schools.summary: Gill draws on David's own history of hiding places and digresses on the courage of lions.
Wesley carries the ambush argument through to the panic a first defeat would cause, and separates the speaker's pretence from his design.
Ellicott describes the difficulty of making the worse appear the better reason; Keil and Delitzsch render the muster from Dan to Beersheba.

sides.position: Every hazard pressed on one side and a riskless plan offered on the other, with flattery assumed as fact
A pretence of slow but sure work, concealing a design to buy David time
The argument from David's known skill at ambush, turned against the first plan

outliers.note: Alone in digressing on the courage of lions, from Hercules to the timid lions of one African town.

9.pericope_label: He is hid now in some pit; let all Israel be generally gathered unto thee

schools.summary: Gill reads the dew for the advantage of numbers and sets out the case of a man shut up in a fortified town.
Clarke doubts the rendering of ropes and prefers the Chaldee; Wesley reads the boast as suited to a vainglorious temper.
Keil and Delitzsch argue the verb of the dew clause and quote Clericus on the vote; Ellicott explains what the hyperbole was for.

debates.question: How is the boast about dragging a city into the brook to be taken?

sides.position: Hyperbole about united Israel's strength, framed to make the advice plausible
A vainglorious flourish, promising it if no other way served
The word for ropes may not mean ropes at all; the Chaldee has towers

outliers.note: Alone in doubting the rendering of ropes, on the ground that no city could be pulled down with cables.

themes: the counsel of Hushai is better
12.pericope_label: We will light upon him as the dew falleth; the LORD defeated the counsel of Ahithophel

schools.summary: Gill traces the route of the message from the council chamber to the priests and the spring.
Henry explains the haste, and reads it as ill with Jerusalem when faithful priests could not be seen entering it.
Clarke writes a lexicographic note on the English word used for the maid, and Wesley gives her a pretext.
Keil and Delitzsch weigh two readings of the clause about destruction; Ellicott canvasses the two candidate sites of the spring.

debates.question: Why send the warning when Hushai's counsel had carried the day?

sides.position: Because the council might change its mind, or had decided after the speaker left
Because acceptance at the moment could easily be exchanged for the other plan

outliers.note: Alone in tracking the English word for the maid through Coverdale, Becke, Cardmarden and Barker, and suspecting King James of restoring it.

15.pericope_label: Thus did Ahithophel counsel; now send quickly and tell David

schools.summary: Gill reports Josephus for a different account of who spotted the couriers, and has the pursuers already know the house.
Wesley infers the season from grain drying in the sun and calls the woman's answer a manifest lie.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the cistern and the covering; Ellicott glosses the grain and the rare word for brook.

debates.question: How is the woman's lie to be judged?

sides.position: A manifest lie, and named as such
Recorded by the historian without comment, like the other cases of women deceiving pursuers

outliers.note: Alone in commending the Latin version for explaining that she appeared to be drying the grain.

18.pericope_label: A lad saw them and told Absalom; the woman spread a covering over the well

schools.summary: Gill notes that the crossing itself was Hushai's advice taken.
Henry reads the unbroken tally as a figure of the Messiah, and the suicide as pride unable to carry an affront.
Clarke refuses the plea of madness, and Wesley reproduces Henry's two summary sentences almost word for word.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both make the suicide a calculation about the cause and the traitor's death waiting for him.

debates.question: What drove Ahithophel to kill himself?

sides.position: Foresight: the cause was lost, and a traitor's death was waiting for him
Wounded pride at seeing his judgement set below another man's
A deliberate act, neither lunacy nor heat, by a man who could expect no mercy

outliers.note: Alone in reading the unbroken tally of the crossing as making David a figure of the Messiah who lost none.

21.pericope_label: Arise and pass quickly over the water; Ahithophel hanged himself

schools.summary: Gill identifies Mahanaim by Jacob's angels and Ishbosheth's reign, and locates Gilead among three tribes.
Clarke states the kinship as sisters' children, both nephews to David, and Wesley marks the delay before the crossing.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both correct Israelite to Ishmaelite from the parallel in Chronicles.

sides.position: An Ishmaelite, as the parallel in Chronicles shows; Israelite is a copyist's error
Simply a man whose son was cousin to Joab, both of them nephews to David

outliers.note: Alone in setting out the difficulty about Abigail's parentage and refusing to decide it.

24.pericope_label: David came to Mahanaim; Absalom made Amasa captain of the host

schools.summary: Gill explains why bedding headed the list and annotates the honey and butter from Homer and the Scythians.
Clarke identifies each article and digresses on the goat-skin satchel; Wesley ends on comfort from strangers.
Ellicott offers two accounts of Shobi and a textual note on the last item; Keil and Delitzsch read the gifts as the first sign of loyalty surviving.

sides.position: A brother of the late Ammonite king, left as governor and now showing gratitude
An Ammonite who had disowned the outrage to David's ambassadors and been spared for it

outliers.note: Alone in describing, from a specimen lying before him, the goat-skin satchel in which parched barley flour was carried.

27.pericope_label: Shobi, Machir and Barzillai brought beds, and wheat, and barley
